A RRIF minimum is a withdrawal rule, not a household spending target

Four graphics separate an ordinary RRIF’s age-based minimum, a gross withdrawal request, a tax budget allowance and the spending assigned to that cash.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore one year of RRIF withdrawals and spending

Interactive planning lab

Minimum for the illustrated year$27,000
Modeled gross withdrawal$30,000
Cash after allowance and assigned spending$4,500

Single-year ordinary RRIF illustration using the All other RRIFs factors reviewed 25 October 2026. RRIF exists before the year begins; annuitant’s whole age at year-start is used, with no spouse-age election, legacy qualifying/pre-1986 treatment or locked-in annuity contract. Minimum = start-of-year fair market value × prescribed factor. Modeled gross withdrawal is the larger of that minimum and the request, capped at the entered balance; no in-year asset-value change is modeled. The selected percentage is only a budget allowance, not prescribed withholding or final tax. No actual tax, benefit interaction, pension splitting, locked-in plan limits or lifetime sustainability is calculated. Negative remaining cash means assigned spending needs another source.

The central idea

Calculate the required gross withdrawal separately from the spending budget. Money leaving a RRIF is not automatically money spent, and a tax allowance is not a tax assessment.

01

Establish which minimum calculation applies

The CRA’s minimum-amount guidance calculates the ordinary minimum from the RRIF’s fair market value at the start of the year and an applicable prescribed factor. The annual minimum begins in the year after the RRIF is established.

This tool assumes the account already exists before the illustrated year, uses the annuitant’s whole age at the beginning of that year, and applies the “All other RRIFs” factor column. It does not calculate an establishment-year minimum, a spouse-age election, legacy qualifying or pre-1986 treatment, or the special calculation for locked-in annuity contracts held inside a RRIF.

Confirm the applicable account category, age basis and opening value with the carrier before using an actual withdrawal figure. The source table and Income Tax Regulations section 7308 were reviewed for this article on 25 October 2026.

02

Apply the factor to opening assets

For the stated ordinary case, the factor below age seventy-one is one divided by ninety minus the beginning-of-year age. The table supplies the later factors, including 5.28% at age seventy-one, 5.40% at seventy-two and 20% at ninety-five or older.

The default opening value is CAD 500,000 and the year-start age is seventy-two. Multiplying by 5.40% produces a CAD 27,000 minimum for the illustrated year. The factor is a withdrawal rule; it does not describe an investment return or a personally sustainable spending rate.

The factor graphic presents the rule table across ages, rather than projecting an account over those ages. The opening value is not assumed to remain CAD 500,000 for the rest of a person’s life. This is a single-year illustration with no future balance path.

03

Compare the request with the modeled gross withdrawal

The entered gross withdrawal request is CAD 30,000. Because it exceeds the CAD 27,000 minimum, the modeled gross withdrawal is CAD 30,000. A request below the minimum is lifted to that minimum in this ordinary example.

The tool also caps the modeled withdrawal at the entered asset balance. That cap reflects its simplified assumption of no in-year change in asset value. It is not a calculation of account liquidity, a sale order or confirmation of how much an actual portfolio can produce on a particular date.

The bars display all three amounts so the request is not silently confused with the modeled withdrawal. If opening assets are zero, both the minimum and available gross withdrawal are zero. The separate spending input can still show an unfunded requirement.

04

Bridge gross cash to a separate spending assignment

The default budget allowance is 25% of the modeled gross withdrawal, or CAD 7,500. Subtracting it from CAD 30,000 leaves CAD 22,500 for comparison with CAD 18,000 of assigned net spending. The ledger therefore shows CAD 4,500 of cash remaining unassigned.

The 25% allowance is a hypothetical budgeting choice. It is not a prescribed withholding rate, an estimate of final income tax, a tax-credit calculation or a prediction of a refund. An actual tax calculation needs the wider household facts and applicable rules.

The spending entry is the part of the household budget assigned to this RRIF cash, rather than necessarily the entire household’s expenses. A positive remainder is not automatically consumed or invested elsewhere. A negative remainder means the assigned spending needs another source under the selected allowance.

05

Keep withdrawals, assets and spending distinct in the wider plan

The matrix varies year-start ages and assigned spending while retaining opening assets, the requested gross amount and the assumed allowance percentage. Each cell is cash left or extra funding needed for one year. Gold negative cells and teal positive cells are signed cash positions.

Where the minimum exceeds the gross request, the model increases the withdrawal. That may create cash beyond the assigned spending amount. A transfer out of a registered account and a household purchase are different events; the remainder needs its own destination rather than being counted twice.

The tool does not calculate benefit interactions, pension splitting, restrictions on locked-in plans, actual withholding, final tax or lifetime sustainability. Review those separately using current rules and account information. The four graphics clarify the relationship between one year’s minimum and its budget without turning the minimum factor into a retirement withdrawal recommendation.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. The prescribed-factor graphic presents federal RRIF rules reviewed on the stated date. The other graphics combine those rules with hypothetical assets, withdrawals, spending and a budget allowance; they are not personal tax calculations. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
